query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy with an increased Cr content (and possibly a minor addition of Hf) will, under hot dip aluminum plating conditions, form an in situ protective Cr‐rich phase (such as a stable Cr-rich oxide or intermetallic phase) that acts as a diffusion barrier against molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a baseline composition similar to AlCoFeNi or other standard HEAs) that does not exhibit a robust protective surface layer when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by increasing the Cr content (with possible Hf addition) to promote the formation of a self‐protecting phase during high‐temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Continuous or repeated contact with high-temperature molten aluminum (temperatures above 660 °C) as experienced in hot dip aluminum plating processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a Cr‐rich oxide or intermetallic layer (for example, a phase analogous to Cr2Ta) that adheres to the substrate and impedes further aluminum attack.
generation.mechanism: At the operating temperatures, the enhanced Cr (and Hf) content reacts with residual oxygen or alloying elements to form a stable, adherent barrier layer. This protective layer restricts the dissolution and wetting of the base alloy by molten aluminum, thereby reducing erosion and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit significantly lower erosion rates and improved corrosion resistance in molten aluminum compared to the conventional material, leading to an extended service life for plating equipment parts.
generation.baseline: Standard materials used in plating equipment that do not form a self-healing protective layer and therefore suffer from accelerated corrosion and erosion under molten aluminum contact.
generation.boundary: The protective effect depends on achieving the optimal Cr (and Hf) concentration to ensure continuous layer formation; deviations in composition or processing may not yield the expected barrier. Additionally, phase stability and adhesion of the protective layer under long-term service conditions remain potential challenges.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold levels of Cr (and Hf) required and the precise nature and effectiveness of the protective phase in the specific molten aluminum environment are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set using the standard refractory HEA composition and another set with the increased Cr (and optional Hf) content. Expose both sets to laboratory-simulated hot dip aluminum plating conditions (i.e., immersion in high-temperature molten aluminum above 660 °C for a prolonged period). Monitor and compare the development of surface layers, erosion rates, and microstructural stability using techniques such as SEM/EDS, in situ XRD, and weight-loss measurements.
measurements: Thickness, continuity, and composition of any protective surface layer (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Microstructural phase analysis before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy with increased Cr (and Hf) does not show a statistically significant reduction in erosion or formation of a continuous, protective barrier layer compared to the baseline alloy under identical conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Early studies in refractory high‐entropy alloys focused on optimizing strength and high‐temperature performance via processing routes such as casting, HIP, and powder metallurgy. Researchers then turned to composition design – adding elements like Cr or Hf – to induce in‐situ precipitation (e.g., formation of Laves phases or stable oxides) that enhanced oxidation resistance and microstructural stability. While these efforts improved performance in harsh thermal and mechanical environments, none of the earlier papers specifically addressed the unique chemical attack posed by long‐term contact with molten aluminum.
decision.unsolved: A key unresolved issue is ensuring that the material remains chemically inert and resistant to erosion when continuously exposed to high‐temperature liquid aluminum. In particular, developing an alloy or coating that forms a robust, self‐protecting interfacial barrier against aluminum attack remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: Adjust the refractory high‐entropy alloy composition by increasing Cr (and possibly Hf) content to promote the in‐situ formation of a protective, adherent phase (such as a Cr‐rich oxide or intermetallic, e.g., Cr2Ta) during service at high temperature.
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend of tailoring alloy compositions to trigger beneficial precipitation and oxidation behaviors that enhance performance. By deliberately formulating a refractory alloy that develops a stable, corrosion‐resistant surface layer under hot dip conditions, the research directly targets the challenge of molten aluminum erosion while leveraging proven concepts from recent advances in high-entropy alloy design.
